articles.title: When to Hire a Fractional CFO
articles.question: What changed in the company that creates a need for senior finance ownership?
articles.role: Timing trigger; keep the full role-and-fit assessment in the CFO guide.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Start with the unowned decision

A fractional CFO may fit when recurring financial decisions need senior judgment and the company can define a workable part-time scope. Begin with the work, its owner, and the availability required; revenue alone does not establish the right staffing structure.

List the next hiring, spending, capital, and board decisions. For each, identify the source information, the person who interprets it, and the person authorized to decide. A current forecast without an owner for changing its assumptions can be a different gap from an overdue close.

Distinguish a leadership gap from a records gap

Separate transaction processing, reconciliations, close oversight, forecasting, and finance leadership. The existing team may need better handoffs, additional accounting capacity, senior interpretation, or a combination. Titles do not guarantee coverage.

Ask a prospective provider to explain which responsibilities they would own, how they would work with the accounting team, and how availability changes around a board meeting or capital event. Centripetal’s precise engagement scope should be confirmed in the conversation.

Write a scope you can evaluate

Use a short brief: decisions to support; recurring outputs; reporting cadence; existing team; approval boundaries; and response expectations. Compare a fractional engagement, a project, and an internal hire against the same brief.

Illustrative example: if the records are current but management cannot connect a hiring plan to collection timing, the need includes planning and interpretation. If balances cannot be reconciled, the brief also needs accountable accounting work. Neither situation can be resolved by an ARR threshold.

Bring the brief to the finance-leadership guide below. It expands the questions into a comparison of work, continuity, and ownership.

articles.title: Bookkeeper, Controller, CFO: What Your Stage Actually Needs
articles.question: Which finance responsibilities are uncovered by the current team?
articles.role: Responsibility boundaries and handoffs; do not repeat the guide’s overall hiring decision.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Map responsibilities before choosing a title

Bookkeeping, controllership, and CFO work cover different responsibilities, but actual roles overlap. A useful starting map separates recording transactions, owning the close and accounting process, and connecting financial evidence to management decisions. Confirm the scope rather than assuming the title defines it.

Find the missing handoff

Transaction work needs accurate source records and reconciliation. Close oversight needs policies, supporting schedules, review responsibilities, and a dependable reporting calendar. Finance leadership needs assumptions, interpretation, and a connection to the operating and capital plan.

A management recommendation can fail if the underlying balances are unresolved. Equally, reliable statements do not by themselves establish who owns the forward forecast. Document where information changes hands and which person is responsible for exceptions.

Compare coverage using one work list

Take a recent reporting period and the next decision. List the work, who performs it, who reviews it, and where no one is accountable. Include the time and specialist input needed for the actual company; avoid using a generic percentage of tasks as a hiring rule.

Illustrative example: a delayed close and a hiring decision may require both close oversight and planning support. Ask candidates how those responsibilities would be covered, including coordination with legal, tax, and accounting specialists. Management retains the company’s decisions and approvals.

The finance-leadership guide below helps translate this work list into a discussion of scope and availability.

articles.title: Fractional CFO or VP Finance? The Decision Is Complexity, Not ARR
articles.question: When does daily operating ownership change the finance leadership model?
articles.role: Operating ownership and work mix; distinct from the when-to-hire timing article.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Compare continuity and responsibility

A fractional CFO engagement can provide senior finance support within an agreed scope. An internal finance leader may be more suitable when the company needs continuing daily management, execution, and team ownership. The comparison depends on the work and availability required, not a universal ARR or hours threshold.

Make the recurring work visible

Describe the close and reporting cadence, forecast maintenance, decision support, board preparation, and management of the finance team. Identify recurring duties separately from a temporary cleanup or financing project.

Multiple entities, contract complexity, reporting obligations, or cross-functional dependencies can change the work. They do not automatically determine which employment model fits. Ask how each option would cover routine responsibilities and periods of peak demand.

Use current proposals for the cost comparison

Compare the same responsibilities, experience, availability, and expected outputs. For an internal hire, consider compensation, benefits, recruitment, management, and any equity terms. For a provider, consider the agreed scope, additional work, response expectations, and transition arrangements. Obtain current proposals rather than relying on unsourced salary ranges.

Before selecting a structure, document what the founder will hand off and what a future hire should inherit: reporting calendar, models, assumptions, systems, and ownership. The wider guide below gives a practical framework for that brief.

articles.title: Reviewing AI-assisted finance work
articles.question: Who checks and owns the decision supported by an AI finance output?
articles.role: Oversight and accountability; do not duplicate the Finance Scorecard’s broader diagnostic.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Define the task and the review

AI assistance in finance should be evaluated task by task. A useful output needs a traceable source, a check against the underlying records, and an accountable person before it informs reporting or a decision. Capability and reliability depend on the system, data, configuration, and task.

Keep the source beside the output

For an invoice extraction, compare fields with the original invoice. For a variance explanation, verify the period, calculation, and supporting records. For a generated forecast, identify which assumptions came from history, which came from management, and which have no support.

An apparently complete answer can conceal a missing input. Treat a fluent narrative as something to review, rather than evidence that the calculation or interpretation has been verified. Avoid entering company information into a system unless its handling fits the company’s approved use.

Assign the operating responsibility

Illustrative example: an AI-assisted board summary describes a cash decline. The reviewer still needs to connect it to collections, payment timing, and the management response. Record the source schedules and unresolved questions beside the summary.

NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework provides a broader basis for evaluating and managing AI risks. The task checks here are editorial prompts for finance work, not a claim that any particular AI product is suitable or unsuitable.

Begin with a bounded workflow, a defined review step, and a way to track corrections. Use the finance-foundation resource below to identify the ownership and information gaps that automation would otherwise reproduce.

Source for the factual distinction

NIST · AI Risk Management Framework. The preparation framework and illustrative examples are editorial concepts for firm review.

articles.title: The Series A Data Room: Connect the Story to Its Evidence
articles.question: Can an investor trace a reported number back to its evidence?
articles.role: Evidence traceability in the data room; the guide owns the full readiness checklist.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Organize a traceable evidence set

A Series A data room should help a reviewer connect the company’s financial story to current supporting records. Confirm the requested scope, access permissions, and document owners before sharing. Folder completeness does not establish financing readiness.

Build the bridge between headline and source

For each material claim in the presentation or model, locate the source schedule, measurement period, and definition. Recurring-revenue metrics need their own definitions and a bridge to accounting records; they need not equal period revenue in the P&L.

Keep financial statements, customer schedules, ownership records, and relevant agreements consistent by reporting cutoff. Track differences, restatements, and missing items instead of silently replacing files. The investor’s actual request determines the required history and review sequence.

Make the open items manageable

Create an index with document name, period, owner, current version, and open question. Ask counsel and the accounting team to review items within their responsibility. Keep sensitive personnel and contractual records under appropriate access controls.

Illustrative example: the deck and model use different customer start dates. Preserve the explanation, correct the source assumption, and identify which outputs changed. Reorganizing the folders alone will not resolve the inconsistency.

Use the fourteen questions and twenty-four organizing items in the diligence guide below to prepare the evidence review. Adapt the list to the requested process; it is not a universal investor checklist.

articles.title: Beyond the Pitch Deck: Financial Evidence to Prepare
articles.question: Which links between the pitch story and supporting evidence need explanation?
articles.role: Pitch-to-evidence reconciliation; distinguish from recurring board-reporting decisions.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Prepare for verification beyond the headline

After a financing presentation, useful preparation connects the headline metrics, operating assumptions, ownership records, and source evidence. The sequence and scope vary by investor and company; this article offers review questions rather than predicting what every investor will ask.

Start with four evidence bridges

Recurring revenue: state the ARR and CARR definitions, cutoff, and customer schedules. Explain the bridge to recognized revenue instead of assuming those numbers should match.

Customer growth: separate new customers, expansion, contraction, and churn using consistent periods and cohorts. Show material concentration and the contract timing behind it.

Forecast: connect the next operating commitment to its assumption, source, owner, and alternative case. Explain changes from actual performance.

Ownership: reconcile the capitalization schedule to the underlying instruments and approvals with the relevant specialists. Record any unresolved terms or missing records.

Turn questions into a review plan

For each gap, name the evidence needed and the person who can resolve it. Agree the version and reporting period before the documents circulate. A supported explanation of a difference is more useful than forcing unlike metrics to match.

The diligence guide below expands the evidence questions. Use it alongside the investor’s requested scope; neither a polished deck nor a completed checklist establishes funding or approval.

articles.title: After the Raise, Capital Structure Becomes an Operating Decision
articles.question: How would another financing obligation change the post-raise operating plan?
articles.role: Post-raise sequencing and commitments; the debt guide owns lender/readiness evidence.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Start with the use and the obligation

Adding debt after an equity raise is a financing decision that needs company-specific analysis. Define the use of proceeds, compare alternatives, and understand the obligations in the proposed agreement before deciding whether the additional capital fits the operating plan.

Read the terms into the cash plan

Review draw conditions, fees, interest, repayment timing, maturity, security, warrants or other equity terms, reporting requirements, and any covenants actually present. Do not assume every facility has the same terms. Review the documents with counsel and the relevant finance specialists.

Place the proposed obligations beside collections and operating commitments. Model an explicit change in a material assumption, such as delayed receipts or a moved milestone, and identify when a commitment or reporting condition would need attention.

Compare the alternatives using the same assumptions

Show the operating plan with and without the proposed facility, including the cost and timing of alternatives. Keep hoped-for financing distinct from committed availability. Negotiating leverage and terms depend on the actual company, lender, and market; no timing rule guarantees a better offer.

Illustrative example: a facility funds a planned hiring step, but that step depends on a customer implementation. Compare the repayment calendar with the changed receipt date and review the agreement’s conditions before treating the proceeds as additional runway.

The venture-debt guide below supports a preparation discussion. It does not determine borrowing eligibility or whether a particular facility is appropriate.

articles.title: The 13-Week Cash Flow Forecast: What It Shows and What It Hides
articles.question: What can a weekly cash view answer, and what depends on the longer-range plan?
articles.role: Time horizon and model boundaries; the guide owns the working forecast review.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Use the weekly view for dated decisions

A 13-week cash-flow forecast projects receipts and payments by week across the next thirteen weeks. It can make the timing around payroll, collections, vendor commitments, and financing visible. Its usefulness depends on supported assumptions and a reconciled opening balance.

Add the explanation behind the dates

A basic receipts-and-payments grid can leave the reader unclear about collection dependencies, committed versus changeable spending, and the response to an altered assumption. These are additions to the model and review process, not limitations imposed by a thirteen-week horizon.

For a material receipt, connect the expected date to billing milestones, terms, and payment evidence. For a payment, locate the commitment and who can change it. Keep financing assumptions and restrictions visible. Earnings and cash movement are different views, as the SEC’s financial-statement guide explains.

Connect the scenario to the decision

Illustrative example: move a customer receipt until after a planned payroll run while holding the other assumptions constant. Identify the affected week, the evidence needed to support the date, and the commitment leadership would revisit. Avoid choosing an arbitrary delay as a universal stress test.

Compare actuals with the prior forecast and assign an owner to changed assumptions. Connect the near-term view to the longer-range operating model so decisions outside the thirteen-week horizon remain visible.

The cash-forecast review guide below covers five evidence checks and a follow-up worksheet. It supports preparation; it does not calculate or certify runway.

Source for the factual distinction

SEC · Financial statements and cash flows. The preparation framework and illustrative examples are editorial concepts for firm review.

articles.title: Make your forecast explainable
articles.question: Which assumptions and decisions should the forecast make visible?
articles.role: Assumption traceability; distinct from cash timing and invoice dependencies in the guide.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Make the forecast explainable

A useful forecast connects actual results, explicit assumptions, and the operating decisions that follow. Accuracy remains a review concern, but a single output also needs a clear explanation of what would change under a different assumption. Investor expectations vary; the model does not establish trust or approval by itself.

Show the bridge from actual to planned

Document the last actual period, the forecast cutoff, and the sources of the starting balances. Explain why planned growth, hiring, or collections differ from recent results. Distinguish evidence-supported assumptions from management judgments and unresolved estimates.

Separate new revenue, expansion, contraction, and churn where relevant. Connect hiring dates and payment commitments to the cash view. Keep a record of who owns each material assumption and when it was last reviewed.

Choose a scenario that tests a commitment

Change an assumption relevant to the company rather than adding a generic downside percentage. Explain which operating commitment changes first, who can respond, and what evidence would reopen the decision.

Illustrative example: an implementation delay moves billing. Follow the consequence through the receipt schedule and planned spending. The review should reveal both the timing dependency and the responsible owners.

Compare actual performance with the prior forecast and record what changed. Use the cash guide below to review the evidence supporting the model, rather than treating a scenario count as a readiness standard.

articles.title: Board Reporting for Seed and Series A Companies
articles.question: Which decision should the board package support at this meeting?
articles.role: Recurring board decision support; supporting resource is the broader Scorecard until the Board Deck Builder is reviewed.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Open with the decision and the request

A useful board package connects management’s recommendation to the operating evidence, alternatives, and requested input or decision. Adapt the structure and cadence to the board’s agreed agenda. A longer deck does not by itself make the decision clearer.

Keep the evidence connected

Explain what changed since the prior meeting, which assumptions moved, and which previous actions remain open. Keep recurring-revenue definitions, cash timing, and reporting cutoffs consistent across the package.

For the main discussion, identify the evidence needed to compare the options. A hiring proposal might need collections and payroll timing; a revenue discussion might need customer-level retention and implementation status. Include the relevant details rather than adding every available metric.

Close with owners and the next review

Record the discussion outcome, the action owner, the next check date, and the condition that would reopen the decision. Confirm formal approvals through the company’s actual governance process.

Illustrative example: contracted growth supports a hire, but the customer start date moves. Distinguish the signed contract from active recurring revenue and cash collection. Explain which commitment depends on the milestone and who will confirm it.

The Board Deck Structure Builder below produces a focus-specific preparation outline and evidence follow-ups. It does not generate slides, replace the agenda, or determine formal approval requirements.

articles.title: Cash-Flow Evidence for a Lender Conversation
articles.question: Which obligations and receipt assumptions should accompany a lender cash model?
articles.role: Lender-facing evidence and obligations; do not repeat the full 13-week model explanation.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Prepare the obligation and its support

For a financing conversation, connect the cash forecast to the commitments, receipt assumptions, and agreement terms behind it. The lender’s requested evidence varies; a preparation framework cannot predict eligibility or approval.

Separate timing from flexibility

Identify payments already committed and choices still open. Review cancellation provisions and actual decision authority before treating spending as reversible. Connect expected collections to billing milestones, receivables aging, payment behavior, and responsible owners.

Where an agreement contains covenants or reporting conditions, review the actual definitions, dates, and calculation rules with the responsible specialists. Model those conditions using the same assumptions as the operating plan. Do not infer them from a generic venture-debt checklist.

Test the assumption that changes the commitment

An explicit scenario should explain both the cash effect and the management response. A delayed receipt and a customer loss change different parts of the plan, so review them separately where relevant.

Illustrative example: a planned hire depends on a large receipt. Move the receipt date, identify the affected commitments, and document who can act before the payment is due. Record the remaining uncertainty rather than labeling the model lender-ready.

Use the venture-debt guide below to organize the wider evidence. The cash-forecast guide helps check the assumptions; actual lender requirements remain a separate conversation.

articles.title: Reviewing Treasury Controls Before a Board Conversation
articles.question: Can the team demonstrate who can move cash and how exceptions are checked?
articles.role: Control ownership and evidence; the guide owns the wider treasury review.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Review access, obligations, and account arrangements

A treasury review should explain where company cash is held, what is available for use, who can authorize movement, and how exceptions are detected. The review scope and duration depend on the accounts, products, and controls involved.

Distinguish a deposit from an investment

Identify the legal owner, bank, product, and any sweep arrangements for each balance. FDIC coverage depends on the insured institution and ownership category; opening another account at the same bank does not automatically create additional coverage. Money market deposit accounts and money market mutual funds are different products. The FDIC’s guidance explains which products are insured.

Use the bank’s product documents and current FDIC guidance to verify the actual arrangement. A yield feature does not by itself establish coverage, liquidity, or appropriate risk.

Check the controls in actual practice

Review authorized users, authentication, approval limits, vendor-payment changes, and exception alerts. Confirm whether a second approval is required and whether it is working as intended. Document who reviews access when people or responsibilities change.

Keep an account inventory, available-cash schedule, control owners, and a dated exception log. Agree a review cadence and revisit it after material changes. This is continuing operational work, not a one-time setup guaranteed to take thirty minutes.

The treasury guide below expands the organizing questions. Specific banking or investment choices require review of the company’s needs and actual product terms.

Source for the factual distinction

FDIC · Deposit insurance at a glance. The preparation framework and illustrative examples are editorial concepts for firm review.

articles.title: CARR vs ARR: When the Definition Matters
articles.question: Which definition and contract timing explain the gap between contracted and live recurring revenue?
articles.role: Metric definition bridge; do not become a generic ARR glossary or repeat diligence checklist.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Keep the metrics and accounting view distinct

ARR describes an annualized recurring-revenue run rate using a stated operating definition. CARR adds contractually committed future recurring revenue under a stated policy. Neither metric is the same as revenue recognized in the financial statements. Stripe’s explanation distinguishes these views.

State the cutoff and inclusion rules

Document what counts as active, which signed contracts or expansions are included in CARR, and how known cancellations or contractions are handled. Identify treatment of usage-based revenue, services, implementation fees, and contract start dates. Keep the same definitions across reporting outputs.

Build a customer-level bridge that distinguishes contracted value, activation, billing, recognized revenue, and cash receipts. A signed agreement does not imply that all five occur on the same date. Ask the accounting owner to confirm recognition treatment for the actual contracts.

Explain differences instead of forcing equality

Illustrative example: a subscription is signed before implementation starts. Depending on the documented metric policy, it may be included in contracted recurring revenue before the active run rate. Its accounting recognition and collection dates follow their own conditions.

Reconcile each metric to its source schedule and explain the bridge to the accounting view. There is no blanket 1–2% tolerance that makes differences acceptable, and ARR need not equal a period revenue line.

Use the diligence guide below to organize definitions, source schedules, and reporting cutoffs. A clear bridge supports review without predicting how a particular investor will respond.

Source for the factual distinction

Stripe · Committed recurring revenue and related metrics. The preparation framework and illustrative examples are editorial concepts for firm review.

articles.title: Customer Concentration: Connecting Exposure to a Decision
articles.question: What operating decision changes if a material customer renews late or leaves?
articles.role: Customer dependency and contract exposure; the guide owns the broader cash review.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Define the exposure before judging it

Customer concentration describes how much of a stated business measure depends on a limited number of customers. Review it alongside renewal terms, payment timing, delivery commitments, and alternatives. A universal percentage cannot establish whether the company is investable.

Show more than one denominator

State the period and measure used for the largest customer and selected customer groups. Recurring-revenue concentration, recognized-revenue concentration, and near-term receipt concentration answer different questions. Keep the customer identifiers consistent with the underlying schedules.

Add the contract and relationship context: renewal dates, termination provisions, implementation dependencies, disputed receivables, and relevant account history. Do not treat a long contract or a strong relationship as proof that a payment or renewal is certain.

Separate delayed payment from customer loss

A delay changes receipt timing. A loss can change future recurring revenue, collections, and delivery costs. Model the relevant case and identify the first commitment affected, the responsible owner, and the evidence that would change the response.

Illustrative example: a customer represents a modest share of annual recurring revenue but most of the cash expected before a payroll run. A revenue-share chart alone would not reveal that timing dependency.

The cash-forecast guide below connects customer dependence to dated commitments. Use its follow-up worksheet to prepare the evidence review.

articles.title: Testing the durability of a vertical SaaS acquisition advantage
articles.question: Does the acquisition plan depend on a channel the company can repeat?
articles.role: Channel mix and repeatability; belongs to finance operations/growth metrics without a new top-level category.
articles.editorial_state: Concept draft; content and factual review pending
articles.editorial_review: Evidence-focused editorial pass completed October 9, 2026. Firm voice, examples, scope and publication approval remain pending. No personal authorship or investor outcome is asserted.
articles.body_html:
Test the source of the apparent advantage

A vertical SaaS company may acquire early customers through founder relationships or industry referrals. Whether that produces a durable acquisition advantage is a question for the company’s own data. An early blended CAC does not establish superiority to horizontal SaaS or predict future channel costs.

Compare channels and cohorts consistently

Define the costs included, allocation method, customer cohort, and period before comparing customer-acquisition costs. Track how founder involvement, referral volume, paid channels, and sales capacity change over time. Explain attribution gaps and small samples.

When evaluating payback, document the revenue and margin basis and the lag between acquisition spending and new customers. Compare like periods and cohorts rather than reading a shift in mix as proof that one channel became less efficient.

Connect the evidence to the next investment

Illustrative example: early wins come through the founder, while the next growth plan assumes a repeatable paid channel. Separate the historical relationship channel from the proposed channel and test its assumptions before applying the early blended CAC to the entire forecast.

A change in CAC might reflect mix, spending timing, contract values, retention, or attribution. Investigate the components before calling it the half-life of an advantage.

Use the finance-foundation resource below to identify the source schedules and owners behind the growth assumptions. Firm-specific examples and external benchmarks remain for editorial review.
